title: Budget to be $15b better due to super: Chalmers
full_text:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the next federal election will be an existential moment for compulsory superannuation, as he reveals new figures showing the long-term budget cost of the age pension will be $15 billion a year less in today's dollars due to more people being able to fund their own retirement.
With One Nation and the Coalition both canvassing weakening the 12 per cent compulsory superannuation contribution, Chalmers has brought forward part of Treasury's intergenerational report, due for release on September 21, to warn against meddling, saying the cost will be borne by today's young adults and those who come after them.
He will tell the Super Members Council on Wednesday that by 2066, which is the end of the report's 40-year forecast period, there will be 9 million age pensioners in Australia, almost double the current number.
But because of the superannuation system now at maturity, Treasury estimates the budgetary cost of the benefit will decrease from today's rate of 2.3 per cent of GDP to 1.8 per cent, a $15 billion saving in today's money based on GDP of around $3 trillion.
By comparison, the GDP pension burden in other OECD economies is estimated to be 10 per cent in the UK, 8 per cent in Canada, 7 per cent in New Zealand, and 6 per cent in the US.
"Super takes serious pressure off social security outlays, and makes the budget much more sustainable as a consequence," Chalmers will say.
On Monday, Hanson gazumped the Coalition by announcing a policy in which workers struggling with the cost of living and who either paid rent or had a mortgage could access 3 percentage points of their 12 per cent compulsory superannuation contribution for a maximum of three years.
On Tuesday, The Australian Financial Review revealed that One Nation's plan was almost identical to a policy hatched by former Liberal leader Sussan Ley. She intended to announce it in her reply to the May budget, but she was rolled for the leadership by Angus Taylor in February.
There remains significant support inside the Coalition for such a policy or something similar and the spectre of Taylor being gazumped by One Nation for the second time in three weeks, the first being the tobacco excise cut, began to cause frustrations.
One MP, speaking on condition anonymity, said Taylor needed to be more fleet of foot and that meant behaving more like an opposition leader than someone in government.
Chalmers said on Tuesday that the policy similarities showed both parties were on the same page when it came to wanting to dismantle the system.
"The next election will be super's existential moment," he will say on Wednesday. "It will help determine whether we make the most of our intergenerational advantages or trash them. 'The crazy announcement by One Nation and the supportive comments from parts of the Coalition have made this very clear. They will end super as we know it and millions of workers will be poorer."
The Coalition super policy, which was never formally ratified by the shadow cabinet, would similarly enable a worker to withdraw 3 percentage points of their super. Unlike Hanson's proposal, however, there would be no time limit on how long the opt-out provision could be used.
Also, under the One Nation proposal, the extra money would be paid to the worker by the superannuation fund, meaning it would only be subject to the 15 per cent concessional tax rate.
Under the Coalition proposal, the employer would pay the money directly to the employee and tax would be levied at the relevant marginal rate. This would raise about $1 billion a year. The policy was slated to start on July 1, 2028, straight after the next federal election.
The intergenerational report, first delivered in 2002 by Liberal treasurer Peter Costello, was a supposed to be released every five years and with the aim of forecasting budget pressures 40 years into the future. The Albanese government now releases the report every term of government.
